title: Progress and Its Price
theme: Consequences: how solutions create new problems
objectives: I can use ten words to describe what follows an action: its consequences, how they build, and whether they can be undone.
I can tell apart verbs that describe a problem getting worse, such as exacerbate, compound, and perpetuate.
I can use the prefixes in-/ir- (not), re- (back), and pre- (before) to read hard words.
I can write an argument about the possible consequences of a decision using at least four words from this unit.
rationale: The year closes on reasoning about long-term consequences, which pulls together the ethics, history, science and technology units. The ten words name what follows an action (ramification, repercussion, precedent), how effects build or cannot be undone (cumulative, inevitable, irreversible), and how a fix can fail or a problem can grow (backfire, exacerbate, perpetuate, compound). Three words are deliberately close in meaning (exacerbate, compound, perpetuate), so students must choose the verb that fits whether a problem is made worse, added to, or kept going. The passage uses two well-documented cases of solutions with unplanned costs and asks students to carry the questions Who else is affected? and What could go wrong? into any decision.

words.def: A complicated result or consequence of an action, often one that no one expected.
words.ex: The ramifications of the new law reached far beyond the town where it was passed.
words.ex2: Before closing the factory, the owners studied the ramifications for workers, suppliers, and local shops.
words.nonExample: A single, obvious result that everyone predicted is rarely called a ramification.

apps.academic: Historians trace the ramifications of a treaty, such as how it changed borders, trade, and daily life.
apps.spoken: I had not thought about the ramifications of skipping practice.
apps.writing: Use ramifications in the plural to point to several linked results, and name at least two of them.

cloze.s: Neither the mayor nor the council had thought about the ___ of closing the only bridge, which cut off the hospital for hours.

cloze2.s: A small change to the bus schedule had large ___ for students who worked after school.

misuse.s: The ramification of the decision was that nothing at all happened to anyone.
misuse.why: A ramification is a consequence; nothing happening to anyone means there was none.

visual.alt: A branching diagram with one decision splitting into many results.

words.def: An unwelcome result of an action or event, often one that comes later.
words.ex: Cheating on the exam had serious repercussions: she lost her place on the honor roll.
words.ex2: The repercussions of the storm lasted for months, as roads stayed closed and crops were lost.
words.nonExample: A reward for good work is not a repercussion.
words.rel: a result that comes back around

apps.academic: Economists study the repercussions of a tax change on prices and jobs.
apps.spoken: If you break the rule, there will be repercussions.
apps.writing: Repercussion usually points to a negative result, so pair it with the action that caused it.

cloze.s: The company's decision to cut safety checks had terrible ___ when a machine failed and workers were hurt.

cloze2.s: Ignoring the warning had ___ for the whole team, which lost the game and its place in the finals.

misuse.s: The repercussions of the storm happened three months before it arrived.
misuse.why: A repercussion follows an event, so it cannot come before the storm.

visual.alt: A large wave beside an impact burst.

words.def: Certain to happen and impossible to avoid.
words.ex: With the river rising for three days, a flood seemed inevitable.
words.ex2: Some mistakes are inevitable when you are learning something new.
words.nonExample: A traffic jam that careful planning could have avoided was not inevitable.

segs.m: able to be avoided (a rare word)

apps.academic: Scientists distinguish between effects that are inevitable and those that careful design could avoid.
apps.spoken: It was inevitable that we would get wet in that storm.
apps.writing: Inevitable is a strong word, so check that nothing could really have prevented the outcome.

cloze.s: After the team lost its three best players, defeat in the final seemed ___.

cloze2.s: As the sun set behind the mountains, the long, cold night became ___.

misuse.s: The cancellation was inevitable, so everyone could easily have avoided it.
misuse.why: Inevitable means impossible to avoid; saying everyone could avoid it contradicts the word.

visual.alt: An arrow that leads in only one direction, with no way to turn aside.

words.def: An earlier event, decision, or case that is used as an example or a guide for later ones.

senses.def: In law, a court's earlier decision that guides how later, similar cases are decided.
senses.example: The judge followed the precedent set by an earlier case about school dress codes.

words.ex: Allowing one student to retake the test set a precedent that others soon asked to follow.
words.ex2: The mayor feared that breaking the rule for one friend would create a precedent.
words.nonExample: The first time anything ever happens cannot follow a precedent, because there is no earlier case.
words.rel: an earlier case that guides a later one

apps.academic: Courts rely on precedent, so a decision in one case guides decisions in later, similar cases.
apps.spoken: If I let you do it, it sets a precedent.
apps.writing: Say what the precedent is and what later choices it might shape.

cloze.s: The principal worried that letting one class skip the exam would set a ___ for every other class.

cloze2.s: The court's decision became a ___ that judges cited in similar cases for decades.

misuse.s: The precedent was a rule that would not be made until twenty years after the decision.
misuse.why: A precedent comes earlier and guides later cases; a rule made twenty years afterward cannot guide the decision.

visual.alt: A balance scale beside a stack of law books.

words.frame: That decision could set a precedent for ___.

words.def: Not able to be undone or changed back to the way it was.
words.ex: Cutting down an ancient forest can cause irreversible damage, since the trees take centuries to regrow.
words.ex2: Once the glass shattered on the floor, the break was irreversible.
words.nonExample: A chalk drawing that can be wiped away is not irreversible.

morph.note: The prefix in- becomes ir- before r, and the final e of reverse is dropped before -ible.

apps.academic: Some medical procedures are irreversible, so doctors ask patients to consider them carefully.
apps.spoken: Think first, because this decision is irreversible.
apps.writing: Use irreversible only for changes that cannot be undone; for a hard-to-fix change, say difficult to reverse.

cloze.s: Because the building was demolished, the loss of the historic landmark was ___.

cloze2.s: Spilled ink on the old manuscript caused ___ damage, since the words could no longer be read.

misuse.s: The irreversible change was easy to undo with one button, and everything was exactly as before.
misuse.why: Irreversible means impossible to undo; a change that one button reverses is the opposite.

visual.alt: A rewind symbol crossed out with a red prohibition sign.

words.frame: An irreversible decision is one that ___.

words.def: Growing larger or stronger as one thing is added to another over time.
words.ex: The cumulative effect of small daily choices, such as sleeping little and skipping breakfast, can be large.
words.ex2: The final exam is cumulative, so it covers everything the class has studied since September.
words.nonExample: A one-time event that leaves no mark on later days is not cumulative.

apps.academic: A cumulative exam tests everything covered so far in a course, not just the latest unit.
apps.spoken: The effect is cumulative: every little bit adds up.
apps.writing: Use cumulative to stress that small things add up over time.

cloze.s: Each sip of soda seems harmless, but the ___ effect over many years can damage teeth.

cloze2.s: The final exam is ___, so it covers every unit we have studied since September.

misuse.s: A cumulative effect is one that happens once and never grows or builds on anything else.
misuse.why: Cumulative means building up as things are added over time; a one-time effect that never grows is not cumulative.

visual.alt: A rising graph beside a growing stack of bricks.

words.def: To produce the opposite of the result you wanted, often harming the person who tried it.

senses.def: To make a loud bang because fuel burns at the wrong time, as an engine can.
senses.example: The old truck backfired with a loud bang.

words.ex: The prank backfired when the teacher laughed and made the class clean up the mess.
words.ex2: Her plan to save time by skipping the instructions backfired, and the shelf collapsed.
words.nonExample: A plan that works exactly as intended does not backfire.

morph.note: A compound of back and fire.

words.rel: a plan that turns against its maker

apps.academic: Policies can backfire when people respond in ways their authors did not predict.
apps.spoken: My joke backfired, and nobody laughed.
apps.writing: Say what the plan was meant to do and what happened instead, so the word shows a contrast.

cloze.s: The company's attempt to hide the problem ___ when reporters discovered it and made it front-page news.

cloze2.s: His plan to win the game by playing recklessly will ___ if the referee keeps handing out penalties.

misuse.s: The plan backfired by working perfectly and giving everyone exactly what they wanted.
misuse.why: To backfire is to cause the opposite of what was wanted; a plan that works perfectly does not.

visual.alt: A flame with an arrow that bends back toward its source.

words.def: To make a bad situation or problem worse.
words.ex: Scratching a mosquito bite can exacerbate the itching.
words.ex2: The drought was exacerbated by a long, hot summer.
words.nonExample: Treating a wound promptly does not exacerbate it; it helps it heal.

apps.academic: Cutting down trees on a hillside can exacerbate flooding by removing the roots that hold the soil.
apps.writing: Exacerbate acts on a problem that already exists, so name the problem first.

cloze.s: Eating a large spicy meal right before bed can ___ heartburn.

cloze2.s: Skipping practice would only ___ the team's problems, because weak passing was the main reason for the losses.

misuse.s: The medicine exacerbated her cough by curing it completely overnight.
misuse.why: To exacerbate is to make a problem worse; curing a cough is the opposite.

visual.alt: A flame with an arrow pointing upward.

words.def: To keep something going, especially something harmful or unfair, so that it continues for a long time.
words.ex: Telling the same stereotype over and over perpetuates it.
words.ex2: The old law perpetuated unfair treatment of workers for decades.
words.nonExample: Challenging an unfair rule helps to end it, not perpetuate it.

apps.academic: Historians show how unfair laws can perpetuate inequality long after the people who wrote them are gone.
apps.spoken: Please do not perpetuate that rumor.
apps.writing: Perpetuate often carries a negative sense, as in perpetuate a myth, so name what is being kept alive.

cloze.s: Every time someone repeats the false rumor, they ___ it for another week.

cloze2.s: Unequal funding for schools can ___ gaps between neighborhoods year after year.

misuse.s: The committee wanted to perpetuate the unfair rule, so it voted to end it immediately.
misuse.why: To perpetuate is to keep something going; voting to end the rule does the opposite.

visual.alt: A circular arrow beside an hourglass.

words.frame: A rumor or habit is perpetuated when ___.

words.def: To make a problem or difficulty worse by adding something to it.

senses.def: A substance made of two or more elements joined together.
senses.example: Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen.

words.ex: He compounded his mistake by lying about it.
words.ex2: A missed bus compounded the day's troubles when the rain began to fall.
words.nonExample: Fixing a mistake right away does not compound it.
words.rel: adding a problem on top of a problem

apps.academic: Hurried repairs can compound a design flaw by hiding it until it fails again.
apps.spoken: Do not compound the problem by panicking.
apps.writing: Compound needs a problem as its object, as in compound the error or compound the difficulty.

cloze.s: Arriving late was bad enough, and forgetting the permission slip only served to ___ the problem.

cloze2.s: The coach did not want to ___ the team's low morale by criticizing every mistake.

misuse.s: To compound the problem, the workers solved it quickly and left nothing else to fix.
misuse.why: To compound a problem is to add to it; solving it quickly adds nothing.

visual.alt: A plus sign beside a warning triangle.

words.frame: He compounded the problem when he ___.

passage.title: When Solutions Bite Back
paras: Every solution is a bet on the future. People solve a problem, and the solution changes the world in ways no one planned. The ramifications of a decision, the many results that branch out from it, are often harder to see than the decision itself. A repercussion is one of those results, usually an unwelcome one that arrives later.

In 1935, scientists in Queensland, Australia, released about a hundred cane toads to eat beetles that were damaging sugar cane. The plan backfired. The beetles lived high on the plants, out of the toads' reach, and the toads spread across northern Australia, where their poison harmed animals that tried to eat them. Today the toads number in the millions, and the damage is, in practice, irreversible.

Some consequences build slowly. Antibiotics, which became widely available in the 1940s, have saved countless lives. But when people use them when they are not needed, the bacteria that survive pass on their resistance, and the cumulative effect of millions of small choices is that some drugs no longer work. Careless use can exacerbate the very problem the drugs were meant to solve.

Not every side effect means a plan has failed, and some costs may be inevitable. Even a careful decision can set a precedent, an earlier case that people point to when they make later choices. A flawed precedent can perpetuate a mistake for decades, because each new decision copies the last one. And a hurried fix for a first problem can compound it, adding a second problem on top of the first.

None of this means that people should stop trying to solve problems. It means they should ask, before they act: Who else will this affect? What could go wrong? How will we know if it does? Progress that comes with an honest price list is progress we can afford.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word “backfired” most nearly means
choices: produced the opposite of the result that was wanted
made a loud noise like an engine
was repeated in other places
was approved by many experts
qs.why: The toads were released to control beetles, but they did not reach them and instead spread and harmed other animals, which is the opposite of what the scientists wanted.

qs.q: Why did the cane toads fail to control the beetles?
choices: The toads quickly died out in Australia.
The scientists released too many toads.
The beetles lived high on the plants, out of the toads' reach.
The beetles were protected by poison.
qs.why: The passage says the beetles lived high on the plants, out of the toads' reach.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that the problem with antibiotics is cumulative?
choices: Antibiotics have saved countless lives.
Antibiotics became widely available in the 1940s.
Some drugs are used only by doctors.
Millions of small choices together led some drugs to stop working.
qs.why: Cumulative means building up over time, and the passage says the effect comes from millions of small choices.

qs.q: In paragraph 4, what does it mean that a flawed precedent can “perpetuate” a mistake?
choices: The mistake is corrected for the first time.
Later decisions copy the earlier one, so the mistake keeps happening.
The mistake is blamed on someone else.
The mistake is quickly forgotten.
qs.why: The passage explains that each new decision copies the last one, which keeps the mistake going for decades.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: People should stop trying to solve large problems.
Scientists cannot be trusted to make good decisions.
Solutions can cause new problems, so people should consider possible consequences before they act.
Animals should never be moved from one place to another.
qs.why: The passage gives examples of solutions with unplanned costs and ends by asking questions people should consider before acting.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words that name what follows an action, how consequences build or cannot be reversed, and how solutions go wrong. They compare three close verbs (exacerbate, compound, perpetuate), practice reading inevitable and irreversible through their prefixes, and read an informational passage about two well-documented cases of unplanned consequences. The unit is the capstone of the year: it asks students to carry questions about consequences into the ethical, historical and technological decisions they studied earlier.

notes.va.ramification.n: Ramification is a consequence that branches out, and it is usually plural. It comes from a Latin word for branch (ramus); mention it as a memory aid. Ask students to draw a branching diagram of the results of one decision. Do not confuse it with ratification.
notes.va.repercussion.n: Repercussion usually names a negative result that comes later. Contrast with consequence, which is neutral. Students may think it is the same as ramification; a repercussion tends to be a single unwelcome result, while ramifications spread out.
notes.va.inevitable.adj: Inevitable is in- (not) plus a rare word, evitable (avoidable). Students overuse it; ask whether the outcome truly could not have been prevented. Link to the unit on cause and effect: what would have to change for the outcome to be avoidable?
notes.va.precedent.n: Precedent is pre- (before) plus ced (go) plus -ent. In law it is a guide for later cases (shown as a second sense). Use school examples: a teacher who allows one extension may be asked for more. Avoid confusing it with president or precedence.
notes.va.irreversible.adj: Irreversible is ir- (a form of in-, not) plus reverse plus -ible. Students often use it for things that are only hard to fix. Ask whether it can truly be undone: a spilled drink can be cleaned, a cut tree cannot be uncut. The opposite is reversible.
notes.va.cumulative.adj: Cumulative means adding up over time. Show with a jar that fills drop by drop. In school, a cumulative exam covers the whole course. Compare with accumulate. Ask for a small habit that has a cumulative effect.
notes.va.backfire.v: Backfire is a compound of back and fire. The engine sense (a loud bang) is shown as a second sense, and the figurative sense is the one taught. Ask for a plan that backfired and the gap between what was intended and what happened.
notes.va.exacerbate.v: Exacerbate makes an existing problem worse. Do not use it for a new problem. Contrast with compound (add another problem on top) and perpetuate (keep it going). A good test: Did the problem get worse, get added to, or last longer?
notes.va.perpetuate.v: Perpetuate means to keep going, usually something harmful or unfair, and the object is often a rumor, a habit, a myth or an inequality. Link to the adjective perpetual. Ask what it would take to stop a rumor from being perpetuated.
notes.va.compound.v: Compound is a multiple-meaning word. In this unit it is a verb meaning to make a problem worse by adding to it; the chemistry noun is shown as a second sense. Students know compound words, so ask how the verb and noun senses are connected: things put together.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: “The scientists wanted to control beetles and released toads. It backfired: the plan produced the opposite of the intended result. The toads spread, which was a ramification no one planned for. The harm may be irreversible because the toads cannot be taken back. If I ignore a problem, I might compound it; if I repeat a rumor, I perpetuate it; and if I make it worse, I exacerbate it.”
discuss: Which is worse for a community, a problem that is exacerbated or a problem that is perpetuated? Why?
How can a good decision still have a repercussion that nobody wanted?
What questions should a leader ask before setting a precedent?
misconceptions: Exacerbate and compound mean the same thing.
Irreversible means very hard to do again.
A precedent is always a good example to follow.
extend: Research a historical decision (for example, a dam, a law, or an invention) and map its ramifications on a branching diagram.
Write an advice column for a leader about how to avoid compounding a problem, using five words from the unit.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Bring back exploit, exhaust, mitigate and surveillance when students discuss technology and the environment. Revisit the three verbs exacerbate, compound and perpetuate after two days with new scenarios, and in later courses ask students to use ramification and precedent in history and civics writing.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: ramificación/consecuencia, repercusión, inevitable, precedente, irreversible, acumulativo, resultar contraproducente (backfire), agravar/exacerbar, perpetuar, agravar/empeorar (compound).

Fact claims in the passage to confirm: about a hundred cane toads were released in Queensland in 1935 to control beetles on sugar cane; the beetles live high on the plants, out of the toads' reach; the toads spread across northern Australia and their poison harms animals that eat them; they now number in the millions; antibiotics became widely available in the 1940s; resistance spreads when antibiotics are used when not needed.
Morphology: repercussion segmented as re- plus percussion (note: a blow that comes back) and inevitable as in- plus evitable (rare word); confirm both with an etymology source.
Teacher note for ramification says the word comes from a Latin word for branch (ramus); confirm against a dictionary.
Sense boundaries: precedent (general sense taught, legal sense as a second sense); backfire (figurative sense taught, engine sense as a second sense); compound (verb taught, noun as a second sense).
